title: The long view
hook: the Buddha's practice took lifetimes, the stories say
tomorrow: why did monks report a friend for saying 'what bliss'?

segments.voice: Yesterday, come back: the moon behind the clouds was never gone. Mai did it. She told Chị Hạnh the truth about the sick days that weren't. Chị Hạnh said: thank you for telling me. See you Sunday.

A fitness challenge promises a new you by the end of the month. Buddhist stories run on a different clock. Long ago, they say, a hermit named Sumedha came to a town where people were fixing the road for a Buddha named Dipankara. One muddy stretch wasn't finished, and the Buddha was already coming. So Sumedha spread his hermit's cloak over the mud and lay face down in it, so the Buddha could walk across without sinking. Lying there, he saw that he could end his own suffering in that very life. He chose not to.
screen: `A NEW YOU BY THE END OF THE MONTH?` → `SUMEDHA, FACE DOWN IN THE MUD.` → `HE COULD HAVE FINISHED THAT DAY.`

segments.voice: Why not? He wanted to become a Buddha himself, to help others cross too. Dipankara stopped, looked down at him, and foretold it: ages from now, this man will be a Buddha named Gotama. Then, the stories say, came life after life of practice. In the Jataka tales the Buddha-to-be is a monkey, a king, a merchant, a hare, building what Buddhists call the paramis, the perfections, one life at a time. That's the long view, and it's a real teaching: awakening is grown, not grabbed. But the tradition has a second voice. The Satipatthana Sutta says that someone who practices mindfulness well could see the fruit in this very life: within seven years, it says, even within seven days. So one side says: be patient. This path is measured in lives, and one bad month is a pebble on a long road. The other side says: don't hide behind the long road. Practice happens now, and the fruit can come now. The patient voice guards against despair. The urgent voice guards against drift. And Sumedha's story holds both. He chose a road of many lives, and he started it that very morning, face down in the mud.
screen: `DIPANKARA FORETELLS A BUDDHA.` · `THE PARAMIS, BUILT LIFE BY LIFE.` · `THE OTHER VOICE: IN THIS VERY LIFE.` · `PATIENCE, AND A START TODAY.` · then, large: `THE LONG VIEW.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on something that grew slowly: a tree outside the window, the grain in a wooden table, the lines on your own palm. Nobody hurried it. Then close your eyes and sit for the two minutes with no score to keep, one breath and then the next, the way a long road gets walked.
The long view: a path measured in lives, the stories say, not in streaks. Sumedha began his in the mud.
Your line: the long view. Patient with the road, and still walking it today. Day seventeen-sixty, done.

howItsDone: Jataka tales of the Buddha's past lives are told at temples and at home, and Sumedha's vow before Dipankara is remembered as the start of that long road.

chat.says: told chị Hạnh the truth. she said 'see you sunday.' but why do i still mess up after years??
options: the stories give the Buddha many lives to get there. be patient, and keep going today.
awakening takes lifetimes anyway, so ease off and pick it back up next year.
the Satipatthana says seven days, so years of slips means you're doing it wrong.
chat.meaning: Sumedha's road ran life after life, the stories say. The long view is patience with the road, not putting it off: the next step is today.

tie.story: Sumedha lay in the mud for Dipankara and chose a road the stories say took many lives.
tie.friend: Mai can take the long view: years of slips aren't the end, and Sunday is her next step.
tie.you: where could you be more patient with yourself?

Sumedha.meaning: the hermit who, the stories say, became the Buddha ages later

Dipankara.meaning: a Buddha of long ago, in the stories

Jataka.meaning: stories of the Buddha's past lives

paramis.meaning: Pali: the perfections, like generosity and patience, built over lives

Satipatthana Sutta.meaning: the Buddha's discourse on the foundations of mindfulness

Chị Hạnh.meaning: big sister Hanh, the chùa's youth leader

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10 (Satipatthana Sutta: fruit within seven years, even seven days)

notes: Shape: debate (two voices inside the tradition: the long road of many lives vs. fruit in this very life). Mai's storyline: she told Chị Hạnh the truth about the fake sick days (picks up day 1759); Chị Hạnh answered kindly; Mai asks why she still slips after years.

Sumedha paraphrased from Buddhavamsa 2 and the Jataka Nidanakatha: he spreads his garment (bark/antelope skin) on the mud and lies down, loosening his hair; he sees he could end the defilements that day but resolves on Buddhahood; Dipankara foretells he will become Gotama. Voiced simply as 'his hermit's cloak'. The texts give a count of ages; left out on purpose ('ages from now'). Confirm.
Jataka forms named (a monkey, a king, a merchant, a hare): all appear among Jataka births; confirm the list is fair.

MN 10 (and DN 22): the closing passage says one who develops the four foundations could expect the fruit within seven years, down to seven days. Numbers are the sutta's own. Confirm wording of the paraphrase.
Framing of the two voices (patience vs. urgency) is the writer's summary of two emphases within the tradition, not two named schools; confirm the framing.
Surprising fact: in the story, Sumedha could have ended his suffering that same day, and chose the long road.
